## Where these principles come from

Not arbitrary style preferences, mostly grounded in research on how humans actually perceive and compare visual information.

::: {.callout-note}
The preferred visualization choices are the ones that best match how our brains process shapes, lengths, and positions, not just what looks nice.
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Keep your goal in mind"}
A plot for yourself during exploration will look different from a plot built to communicate a finding to an audience.
:::


# Encoding data with visual cues

## Not all visual cues are equal

Several visual channels are available to represent a value: position, length, angle, area, brightness, color hue.

::: {.callout-important title="Human's perception"}
We are quite good at comparing **position and length**. We are noticeably worse at judging **angles**, and even worse at judging **area** alone. Brightness and color hue are the hardest of all to quantify precisely.
:::


## Can you read pie charts?

A pie chart encodes each value with **both** angle and area simultaneously.


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(browsers |> filter(year == "2000"), aes(x = "", y = pct, fill = browser)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) + coord_polar("y") +
  labs(title = "2000", x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_void()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=384}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(browsers |> filter(year == "2015"), aes(x = "", y = pct, fill = browser)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) + coord_polar("y") +
  labs(title = "2015", x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_void()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-2.png){width=384}
:::
:::



## What about bar plots?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(browsers, aes(x = fct_reorder(browser, pct, .fun = mean), y = pct, fill = year)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = seq(0, 30, 10), color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Browser", y = "Percent", fill = "Year",
       title = "Browser share is far easier to compare as a barplot")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



## Exercise

::: {.callout-tip title="Which browser grew the most from 2000 to 2015?"}
Try plotting the pie chart and the bar plot by running the code below
:::


::: {.cell exercise='encoding_ex'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
browsers <- tibble(
  browser = rep(c("Opera", "Safari", "Firefox", "Chrome", "IE"), 2),
  year = rep(c("2000", "2015"), each = 5),
  pct = c(3, 21, 23, 26, 28, 2, 22, 21, 29, 27)
)

ggplot(browsers, aes(x = "", y = pct, fill = browser)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  facet_wrap(~year) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_void()

ggplot(browsers, aes(x = browser, y = pct, fill = year)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge")
```
:::




# Know when to include 0

## Length implies proportionality

- When a visual cue is **length** (as in a bar plot), the reader assumes the length is proportional to the value. 

- If the bar doesn't start at 0, that assumption breaks and a small real difference can be stretched to look huge.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common problem in media"}
This is a favourite trick of misleading charts in the media: truncate the y-axis, and a 16% increase can be made to look like it nearly tripled.
:::

## Exaggerated axis truncation

![](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-1/dataviz/img/class2_8.jpg)


## How to exaggerate an increase?

::: {.callout-tip title="Try playing around with the axis"}
The template below compares my company's profit in 2011 and 2012. Notice how much bigger the increase looks once the y-axis gets truncated. Which plot would you rather show?
:::


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.webr .cell-code}
profit <- tibble(year = c("2011", "2012"), value = c(340, 396))

ggplot(profit, aes(year, value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "firebrick") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(330, 400)) +
  labs(title = "Axis truncated", y = "Dollars (thousands)")

ggplot(profit, aes(year, value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Axis starts at 0", y = "Dollars (thousands)")
```
:::



## Length vs Position



::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(life_exp, aes(x = continent, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 85)) +
  labs(title = "Forced to include 0")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=432}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(life_exp, aes(x = continent, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Zoomed to the data")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-2.png){width=432}
:::
:::



## The rule of thumb

::: {.callout-note title="Is the 0 required here?"}
The empty space between 0 and 50 in the left plot adds no information and makes it harder to see the within-group and between-group variability that actually matters here.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Bars vs Points}
If length is your visual cue (bars), **always** include 0. If position is your cue (points, lines), it's fine (often better) to zoom to the range that matters.
:::

# Do not distort quantities

## Circles

![]{https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-1/dataviz/img/state-of-the-union.png}


## Radius-proportional vs. area-proportional


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.webr .cell-code}
gdp <- tibble(country = c("US", "China", "Japan", "Germany", "France"),
              ratio = c(1, 1/2.6, 1/3.4, 1/4.9, 1/5.8))

ggplot(gdp, aes(x = country, y = 0)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = ratio), shape = 21, fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 30, guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Radius proportional (distorted)") +
  theme_void() + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

ggplot(gdp, aes(x = country, y = 0)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = ratio), shape = 21, fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 30), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Area proportional (correct)") +
  theme_void() + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
`ggplot2`'s `scale_size_area()` defaults to making **area**, not radius,
proportional to the value — the mathematically honest choice. Worth knowing
which default you're getting when you map a value to `size`.
:::

## Just use a different plot!


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(gdp, aes(x = fct_reorder(country, ratio), y = ratio)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "GDP relative to US")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



# Show the data

## Oh Hello?

![]{https://i.pinimg.com/1200x/9b/71/89/9b7189f054526b97684c36ea725d8810.jpg}


## Meet ET

::: {.callout-warning title="How tall are you humans?"}
The extra-terrestrial arrives Earth for the first time. Instead of asking if you have any mass destructive weapons or asking for the most appropriate swear words in human language, the alien asks you: How tall are you guys?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Uh-oh, what do I do?"}
Instead of giving the alien a random answer, you kidnapped 338 women and 812 men. You measured each of their heights in inches, and reported to the alien. But reporting 1450 numbers is too much of a hassle, so you had to show the alien a plot! 
:::


## The Antennae plot

Imagine describing human height to an alien who has never seen a person. A common way to compare two groups (popularized by spreadsheet software) is the **dynamite plot**: a bar at the group mean, with error-bar "antennae".


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
heights |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(height), se = sd(height) / sqrt(n())) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = mean)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey70", width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean, ymax = mean + 2 * se), width = 0.2) +
  labs(y = "Height (in)")
```
:::



## Bar going to 0 means 0-in height?


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



## Can you see the shape of the crowd?



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(heights, aes(x = sex, y = height)) +
  geom_point()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



## Jitter and alpha blending

Two small fixes make an enormous difference when points overlap heavily:

::: {.callout-note title="Jitter"}
`geom_jitter(...)` adds a small random horizontal nudge to each point, spreading out ones that would otherwise land exactly on top of each other. 

- `geom_jitter(width=...)` adjusts the amount of horizontal jitter. 

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Alpha"}
Does anyone recall what does `alpha` change to a plot?

- makes points semi-transparent, so denser regions naturally look
darker.

:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(heights, aes(x = sex, y = height)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, alpha = 0.2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Now the height difference between groups, and the overall shape of each
distribution, are both visible at a glance.

## Exercise

::: {.callout-tip title=""}
Try and run the following code to compare two styles of plots.
:::


::: {.cell exercise='show_data_ex'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
# Data set
heights <- tibble(
  sex = rep(c("Female", "Male"), c(338, 812)),
  height = c(rnorm(338, mean = 64.5, sd = 3.5), rnorm(812, mean = 69.3, sd = 5.4))
)
# Normal plot
ggplot(heights, aes(x = sex, y = height)) +
  geom_point()
# Plot with jitters
ggplot(heights, aes(x = sex, y = height)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, alpha = 1)

```
:::


# Ease comparisons

## Are the men taller than women?



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(heights, aes(x = height)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~sex, scales = "free_x")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



## Same data, Same Binwidth


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(heights, aes(x = height)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~sex)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



## Aligning plots



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(heights, aes(x = height)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~sex, ncol = 1)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



## Align the other way


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(heights, aes(x = sex, y = height)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.15)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Three plots, one dataset

::: {.callout-tip title="Which plot is better?"}
Run the following code to generate three plots we discussed earlier. What kind of question can each plot actually answer?
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.webr .cell-code}
# Antennae plots
heights |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(height), se = sd(height)/sqrt(n())) |>
  ggplot(aes(sex, mean)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey70") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean, ymax = mean + 2*se), width = 0.2) +
  labs(title = "Dynamite plot")

# Stacked histograms
ggplot(heights, aes(x = height)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~sex, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Aligned histograms")

# Boxplot
ggplot(heights, aes(x = sex, y = height)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.15) +
  labs(title = "Boxplot + points")
```
:::



## Summary {.smaller}

- **Position and length** are the visual cues humans read most accurately;
  angle is worse, area worse still, color/brightness hardest of all
- **Always include 0** when the cue is length (bars); it's optional, often
  better skipped, when the cue is position (points)
- **Radius ≠ area** — squaring a linear scale factor silently exaggerates
  differences
- **Show the data**: raw points, jitter, and alpha blending beat a bar +
  error bar summary almost every time
- **Match the axes and align your panels** to the direction of the
  comparison you actually want the reader to make

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
